video_title: Steve Keen: The Economics of Global Warfare
gist: Post-Keynesian economist Steve Keen argues that a Strait of Hormuz disruption from the US/Israel-Iran war is a physical production shock, not just an oil-price shock: because energy and GDP move roughly one-for-one, losing ~10% of world energy plus ~30% of fertilizer, ~50% of helium, ~50% of sulfuric acid and ~50% of lubricating oils implies a downturn twice the size of the GFC, famine risk in food-importing countries, and debt-deflation rather than a lasting inflation spiral. He also lays out his critique of Ricardo's comparative advantage (a word-level sleight of hand he says he found six months ago), the reserve-currency curse behind US deindustrialization and its inability to restock rare-earth-dependent weapons, and argues China's engineer-run, self-sufficiency-driven system will outlast the US through both global warming and an American AI boom-bust.

themes.theme: Energy-GDP Coupling vs Neoclassical Production Theory

insights.claim: Steve Keen argues energy and output move almost one-for-one: a 3% rise in energy use coincides with roughly a 3% rise in GDP, and a 5% fall in GDP with a 5% fall in energy, making energy availability a hard constraint rather than a small cost share.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: If energy volumes cap real output one-for-one, physical energy flow data is a better leading indicator of GDP than price-based or share-weighted models used by consensus forecasters.
insights.quote: uh if there's a change in energy of say energy goes up 3% GDP goes up about 3%

insights.claim: Mainstream models treat energy as roughly 5% of GDP and therefore conclude a 10% loss of energy supply reduces output by only half a percent, because they assume labour and capital can be substituted for missing energy.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Consensus GDP damage estimates from an energy chokepoint closure may understate the hit by an order of magnitude, so positioning built on official forecasts is mispriced.
insights.quote: Therefore 10% fall in energy half a percent fall in GDP who cares fundamentally.

insights.claim: Keen says the Cobb-Douglas production function that underpins mainstream production theory contained statistical errors economists never checked, because they liked its implication that income is distributed meritocratically.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Flags that the analytical machinery behind consensus growth and distribution forecasts rests on an unvalidated model, a reason to discount its shock scenarios.

insights.claim: Keen dates his break with mainstream economics to the theory of the second best, which shows that abolishing trade unions while leaving employer associations and monopolies intact actually reduces social welfare.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Provides the analytical basis for his view that decades of union-weakening deregulation lowered welfare and destroyed the wage pass-through channel that inflation forecasts assume.
insights.quote: it's hard to get rid of the capitalists. So we'll just get rid of the workers instead.

insights.claim: Keen models the economy with system dynamics, the method developed by engineer Jay Forrester in the 1950s, treating it as an interacting, unstable dynamic system rather than a set of equilibria.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Explains why his forecasts feature nonlinear cliffs and cascades rather than the smooth marginal adjustments consensus models produce.

insights.claim: Keen says 71 separate surveys of firms have all found the neoclassical assumption of rising marginal cost to be a myth, with most firms facing constant or falling marginal costs, so real-world profit maximisation means selling as many units as possible and competing on product differentiation rather than price.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: If firms have falling unit costs and list-price behaviour, volume and market share, not marginal pricing, drive earnings, and the welfare case that competitive markets maximise welfare collapses.
insights.quote: the basic profit maximization strategy of real world firms is sell as many bloody units as possible

insights.claim: Keen argues Marx himself destroyed the labour theory of value in the Grundrisse by generalising profit to the gap between the use value and exchange value of any input, which implies an energy-based theory of production because energy is the major input, and that Marx then contradicted his own logic in Capital to preserve the falling rate of profit and the inevitability of socialism.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Grounds his energy-centric production model in a value theory that treats energy, not labour, as the profit-generating input, which is why he reads energy chokepoints as existential rather than marginal.
insights.quote: profit comes from characteristics that labor shares in common with all other commodities and that is that the buyer exploits the use value and pays for the exchange value

themes.theme: Hormuz as a Non-Oil Chokepoint: Helium, Sulfur, Lubricants

insights.claim: Keen estimates roughly 10% of world energy supply flows through the Strait of Hormuz, so a blockage implies a 10% fall in global GDP, about twice the magnitude of the global financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Sets a scale for the tail risk: equity, credit and commodity positioning calibrated to a GFC-sized shock would be half-sized for this scenario.
insights.quote: that's twice the magnitude of the global financial crisis

insights.claim: US refineries were mostly built to process high-sulfur sour crude while American fracking produces sweet crude, so the US exports sweet oil to Asian refineries and reimports products, making Trump's claim that America does not need the Strait of Hormuz false.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: US energy independence claims do not protect domestic diesel and petroleum supply, so US refiners and downstream fuel prices are exposed to a Hormuz closure despite record domestic crude output.
insights.quote: even America is dependent upon this oil, even though Trump claims, you know, we don't use it. That is nonsense.

insights.claim: The timing of the shortage depends entirely on inventory buffers: Keen says China holds about a year and a half of oil supply while America had 90 days and is now down to less than 30.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: A stock gap that wide means the US hits physical shortage within weeks while China can absorb over a year, a direct asymmetry in relative equity, currency and industrial performance.
insights.quote: And China has 1 and a2 years of oil supply. America had 90 days. It's now down to less than 30.

insights.claim: Keen expects the shortage to arrive as a nonlinear cliff rather than a gradual squeeze, with supply going from meeting 100% of demand to about 5% once stocks run out, and prices going through the roof at that moment.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Argues for convex, out-of-the-money exposure to energy prices rather than linear positioning, since the repricing is discontinuous and stock-depletion-timed.

insights.claim: Keen says 50% of the world's helium comes through the Strait of Hormuz and that Iran damaged two of the 14 separation machines in one of the main refineries early in the war, implying roughly a 10% fall in global helium supply, which threatens microchip manufacturing and MRI scanners.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Helium is an unhedged, low-substitutability input to semiconductor fabrication and medical imaging, so a supply cut hits chip output and healthcare capex independently of oil prices.
insights.quote: 50% of the world's helium comes out of the straight of homos

insights.claim: Keen says about half the world's sulfuric acid comes from the region and copper cannot be refined without it, at the same moment the world is consuming copper for a ridiculous number of data centres.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: A sulfuric acid shortage constrains refined copper supply into peak AI-datacentre demand, a squeeze that would show up in copper prices and datacentre build schedules.
insights.quote: you can't refine copper without sulfuric acid. And we're losing like half the world's sulfuric acid.

insights.claim: Keen relays that roughly half the world's lubricating oils come from the Middle East and are no longer flowing, so once existing cans and stockpiles are used up machines simply stop working regardless of energy availability.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Lubricant scarcity is a physical cap on machine uptime across manufacturing and transport, an under-followed input that could throttle output even where fuel is available.
insights.quote: about half the world's lubricating oils come from the Middle East now they're not flowing anymore

insights.claim: Keen says China had been deliberately running its stockpiles down to help supply the rest of the world and is now switching to rebuilding them, which removes a buffer that has so far masked the shortage.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Chinese restocking flips China from a marginal supplier of slack to a competing bidder, accelerating the date at which physical shortages hit Western prices.
insights.quote: China's been running its stocks down deliberately to help out the rest of the world for a while. Now they're deciding to reby them.

insights.claim: Keen expects the combined loss of energy, sulfuric acid, fertilizer and lubricating oils to trash many industries as a death by a thousand cuts hitting the economy within the next couple of months.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Puts a near-term horizon on the thesis, making input-shortage disclosures in Q3 industrial earnings the place to look for confirmation or falsification.
insights.quote: we're going to sort of have a death by a thousand cuts type effect hitting the economy in the next couple of months

themes.theme: Fertilizer Loss and Global Famine Risk

insights.claim: Keen says about one third of the world's fertilizer is produced from the sulfur-rich byproducts of Gulf sour crude refining, so the war implies roughly a 30% fall in global fertilizer supply.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: A 30% fertilizer supply loss would reprice nitrogen and phosphate producers outside the Gulf and lift grain prices with a one-season lag.

insights.claim: Keen argues that without artificial fertilizers global food output would only support about two billion people, so a 30% fertilizer loss translates into a nonlinear, more-than-30% fall in food production against a population of eight billion.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Frames agricultural commodities as facing a physical carrying-capacity shock rather than a cyclical price move, with famine as the clearing mechanism.
insights.quote: Now without fertilizers food output for on the planet would be limited to enough to support about two billion people.

insights.claim: Keen argues rich food importers are not safe in a global rather than localized shortage: the UK relies on imports for more than 40% of its food, and being able to outbid India is no guarantee of supply once exporters restrict sales.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Food-import-dependent developed economies carry unpriced sovereign risk in a global shortage, relevant to UK inflation, gilts and sterling.
insights.quote: There's no longer any guarantee that countries like England, which of course can pay more for food than India, are actually going to be able to buy that food.

insights.claim: Keen cites India's decision three years ago to stop exporting all rice except basmati after a bad harvest as the template for export bans that Russia and Ukraine could repeat, cutting global tradable food supply further.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Export-restriction risk means tradable grain supply can shrink faster than production does, an amplifier for grain price spikes.

insights.claim: Keen reports that Australia, which produces seven times as much food as it consumes, has farmers cutting fertilizer use by half because of cost, which could halve Australian food output and remove a major surplus exporter.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Fertilizer price rationing by farmers is a real-time, observable transmission channel from the input shock to next season's exportable surplus.
insights.quote: Apparently Australian farmers have decided to use half as much fertilizer given the cost of fertilizer.

insights.claim: Keen expects the food shortage to hit Southeast Asia first and thinks the US will avoid famine because it produces much of its own fertilizer, while still facing manufacturing holes such as being unable to refine copper for data centres or make microchips.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Splits the shock geographically: food-driven instability in importing Asia and the UK, input-driven industrial disruption in the US.

themes.theme: Why the Oil Spike Ends in Debt-Deflation, Not Inflation

insights.claim: Keen and Michael Hudson both expect an initial oil-driven inflation spark but not a lasting inflationary spiral, because manufacturers can pass on costs while workers cannot without the trade union bargaining power they had in the 1970s.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Argues against pricing in a persistent 1970s-style inflation regime, favouring a short CPI spike followed by disinflation and demand destruction.
insights.quote: manufacturers can do it. Okay? But workers can't because they don't have the trade unions that used to exist.

insights.claim: Keen's mechanism runs from higher prices with flat wages, to less real purchasing power, to business cash flow below plan, to inability to service interest commitments, and then to price cutting by firms facing bankruptcy.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Points at corporate cash flow versus interest coverage as the transmission variable to watch, favouring credit-quality caution over inflation hedges after the initial spike.

insights.claim: Keen notes that in the Great Depression private debt fell about 10% per annum while prices fell as much and nominal GDP fell 20% per annum, so the debt-to-GDP ratio rose even as debt levels fell, and expects a similar dynamic now.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: If deleveraging raises the debt-to-GDP ratio through falling nominal GDP, leveraged borrowers and mortgage credit deteriorate even as nominal debt shrinks.
insights.quote: the price level drops and that means the outstanding value of private debt rises even though the level of private debt hasn't increased. And that was what gave us the great depression.

insights.claim: Keen predicts workers unable to pay mortgages and firms unable to service working-capital debt, producing bankruptcy spreading across the whole economy and the most severe downturn in demand since the Great Depression rather than merely since the global financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Sets a severity benchmark well beyond 2008 for credit losses, relevant to bank capital, mortgage credit and high-yield spreads.

themes.theme: Reserve-Currency Curse and US Industrial Decline

insights.claim: Keen argues reserve-currency status structurally overvalues the dollar because of monetary demand beyond trade demand, and if the overvaluation is around 30% then American manufacturing prices sit about 30% above comparable foreign producers, which is why production migrated offshore.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Implies tariffs cannot fix competitiveness while the dollar stays overvalued, so reshoring theses need a weaker dollar to work.
insights.quote: American manufacturing prices end up being 30% higher than comparable manufacturing systems elsewhere in the world

insights.claim: Keen offers an empire cycle framework: manufacturing dominance enables military dominance, which makes the currency the reserve currency, which overvalues it, which lets defeated vassal states rebuild manufacturing until they can displace the hegemon, as with the Spanish, Portuguese and Dutch empires.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: A structural, mechanism-based case for secular dollar decline and Chinese industrial ascendancy that does not depend on policy choices.
insights.quote: being a reserve currency is a huge mistake for a glo for a global hedgeimon

insights.claim: Keen argues America will likely be unable to restock the precision weapons expended against Iran because those weapons need refined rare earth minerals for magnets and guidance, China does the refining, and China is refusing to sell them to America.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Rare-earth refining capacity is the binding constraint on US rearmament, making non-Chinese refining projects and munitions supply chains strategically scarce.
insights.quote: China is going is refusing to sell those rare earth minerals to America

insights.claim: Keen contends against Warren Mosler and MMT that exports boost the exporting country's domestic money supply and reduce the importer's, giving exporting companies higher revenue to invest and maintain their technological lead, so trade surpluses genuinely benefit the surplus country as Keynes claimed.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: If surpluses fund reinvestment and compounding advantage, persistent-deficit economies lose industrial capability cumulatively, supporting long-horizon underweights on deficit-country manufacturing.
insights.quote: MMT has this frankly stupid argument that exports are a cost and imports are a benefit

themes.theme: Ricardo's Province Con and the Case for Industrial Policy

insights.claim: Keen says he discovered about six months ago that Ricardo, in the 1817 Principles, switched the word to province where the argument required industry or branches of trade, concealing that specialization requires moving dedicated machinery between industries and not just capital between countries.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: If comparative advantage rests on a textual sleight of hand, the unconditional free-trade welfare claim that anchors trade-policy modelling has no theoretical foundation.
insights.quote: You cannot turn a wine press into a spinning jenny.

insights.claim: Keen argues gains from trade depend on whether investment creates new capital goods in each country at the right time, not on reallocating existing resources, which makes free trade conditional rather than unconditionally welfare-improving and means capital gets written off in any specialization shift.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Reframes trade liberalisation and trade wars as questions about investment rates and capital write-offs, which is where the real earnings impact for industrial firms shows up.

insights.claim: Keen notes that essentially every country that successfully industrialized used tariffs to protect domestic industry, including America banning many British goods, and cites Michael Hudson's PhD thesis on American protectionism, with countries becoming free-trade advocates only after their industry won.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Historical base rate favours protection-plus-industrial-policy for building capacity, so judge tariff programs by whether the domestic build-out policy accompanies them.

insights.claim: Keen argues Trump's tariffs will fail to reshore manufacturing because he only raises barriers without doing anything to encourage domestic manufacturers to take up the slack, and is instead trying to attract foreign manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Predicts tariffs raise input costs without producing the domestic capacity story equity markets are paying for in industrial reshoring names.

insights.claim: Keen says successful industrial policy has to be national and points to Singapore, Malaysia, China, Japan, Korea and post-war Germany as countries that used tariffs plus a range of restrictions to reserve domestic demand for domestic producers and fill holes in their manufacturing systems.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Gives a checklist for judging credible national industrial strategies versus tariff theatre when allocating to domestic-capacity beneficiaries.

insights.claim: Keen uses Honda attaching salvaged bomber motors to bicycles, and Japanese carmakers entering the US market through the small cars American producers refused to build, as an illustration that firms industrialize by exploiting niches incumbents ignore and then reinvesting the proceeds into higher-quality products.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: A repeatable disruption pattern for spotting where low-end foreign entrants, including Chinese manufacturers today, climb into incumbents' core markets.

themes.theme: Trump's Personality as a Market Variable and Energy Geopolitics

insights.claim: Keen says the Iran war is economically bad for the United States and Israel but profitable for a narrow group of the very wealthy, and that Trump welcomes the resulting inflation because his friends sell oil, so removing Saudi and Iranian barrels from the market raises their revenue.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Suggests policy will not self-correct on national economic grounds because the beneficiaries of higher oil prices sit close to the decision-maker.
insights.quote: Why does he love the inflation? Because his friends sell oil.

insights.claim: Keen describes Trump running a pump and dump on markets by declaring the war on and then over, with suspicious trades roughly 15 minutes before announcements as traders pile into oil on the buy side before war-on statements and the sell side before war-over statements.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Implies oil and equity volatility around presidential war statements is a recurring, tradeable pattern with informed flow ahead of the headline.
insights.quote: when the war is going to be back on, people pile in on the on the on the the buy side for oil and when when he says it's over, they pile in on the sell side

insights.claim: Keen uses narcissistic personality disorder as a predictive framework for Trump, arguing a narcissist lies to persuade himself rather than others, can never admit a mistake, and will manufacture attention-getting events such as wars, so pre-election pledges are worthless as guidance.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Means policy announcements should be treated as attention-seeking noise with high reversal probability rather than as commitments to be discounted into prices.
insights.quote: a narcissist doesn't lie to persuade you. They lie to persuade themselves

insights.claim: Keen thinks the Iran war can only end when Gulf states such as the UAE and Kuwait refuse America continued use of their bases, potentially after Iran destroys Gulf state facilities, making Muslim-state solidarity and base access the pivotal variable rather than negotiations.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Identifies Gulf base-access decisions as the leading indicator for war termination and therefore for the energy risk premium.

insights.claim: Keen argues Europe's core economic problem from the Ukraine war is paying far more for American LNG than it paid for Russian pipeline gas, with the Nord Stream pipeline probably destroyed by Ukrainians and German industry going backwards rapidly, so European survival requires a rapprochement with Russia.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Frames European industrial competitiveness as an energy-price problem with a political fix, making any Russia-Europe energy thaw a large positive catalyst for German industrials.
insights.quote: The Americans are doing very nicely selling liquid natural gas to Europe at a much higher price than they were paying to the Russians. And European industry is going backwards very rapidly, especially German industry.

insights.claim: Keen blames NATO expansion past its promised boundaries for provoking the Ukraine conflict while saying Putin overstepped by invading the whole country rather than the Donbass, leaving Russia stuck in a quagmire.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Implies a negotiated settlement requires accepting a neutral buffer, which is the condition under which European energy costs could normalise.

insights.claim: Keen reads the Venezuela intervention as a resource grab for heavy oil, part of an American pattern of dominating oil-producing countries with different political systems, and notes Iran was number five on a target list that also included Iraq, Syria and Libya, with US checks and balances failing to restrain it.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: If resource control drives intervention, oil-rich non-aligned states carry elevated political risk and their production is a persistent source of supply disruption.
insights.quote: the the so-called checks and balances in the American system are bouncing checks

themes.theme: China's Engineer State, Climate Resilience and the AI Boom-Bust

insights.claim: Keen says the most important fact about China is that it is run by engineers rather than economists or lawyers, including Xi with an engineering degree, which makes policy outcome-oriented and experimental, testing different approaches in different regions.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Predicts Chinese policy responses will be physical-capacity-driven rather than ideological, which is why Keen expects them to handle energy, climate and AI shocks better.
insights.quote: the most important thing I say about China is it's run by engineers okay not economists not lawyers

insights.claim: Keen argues the Soviet Union failed because it followed Marx's reproduction schema as reinterpreted by the engineer Feldman, building capital goods while neglecting consumer goods, and input rationing under five-year plans made factories repeat last year's products instead of innovating.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Supplies the historical lesson Keen believes China deliberately learned, explaining its emphasis on consumer-sector innovation and competition.

insights.claim: Keen says Chinese per capita income has been growing about 8% per annum, which no part of the world has ever sustained, producing genuine allegiance to the leadership through rising living standards and a bureaucracy responsive to people's needs.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Argues against the political-fragility thesis on China, which matters for anyone underweighting Chinese assets on regime-risk grounds.
insights.quote: per capita income has been growing by about 8% peranom and that's unheralded

insights.claim: Keen says China deliberately suppresses its financial sector because it believes American problems come from letting finance dominate, so US policy serves the financial sector rather than the American people.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Explains why Chinese policy tolerates lower financial-asset returns in exchange for industrial capacity, a persistent difference in where profits are allowed to accumulate.
insights.quote: China's literally uh suppressing the financial sector. They don't want to be dominated by the finance sector.

insights.claim: Keen recounts seeing the Shenzhen free trade zone being built in 1981-82 with a rule that every foreign company needed a Chinese partner owning half the business within five years, which he realized would build a domestic capitalist class that stays after wages rise and foreign capital leaves.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: The joint-venture ownership requirement is the mechanism by which technology and capability transfer became permanent, the template for judging current market-access bargains.

insights.claim: Keen argues the memory of the Opium Wars, learned by Chinese children the way Americans learn the Civil War, drives a doctrine that the West cannot be relied upon, pushing China toward producing everything it needs domestically including the soybeans and meat it currently imports.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Predicts continued Chinese import substitution regardless of price signals, a structural headwind for exporters of agricultural and industrial goods to China.

insights.claim: Keen says Chinese carbon dioxide output is now falling because nuclear, solar and wind additions outpace new coal plants, expects China to target zero carbon around 2030 to 2040 versus a Paris target of 2050 the West has already breached, and concludes China is the only major country likely to hold its social system together through global warming.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Implies Chinese energy-transition capacity is both a climate-resilience asset and an export franchise, while Western climate commitments should be treated as non-binding.
insights.quote: China will be able to keep itself going with non-carbon based energy

insights.claim: Keen expects an American AI boom and bust along Schumpeterian lines because every company entering a new technology aims to be the last one standing, producing massive overinvestment, and notes AI costs are currently roughly five to ten times revenue.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: A cost-to-revenue gap of that size implies a bankruptcy wave and slump ahead of broad AI diffusion, arguing for caution on AI capex beneficiaries.
insights.quote: the costs are about 10 times the revenue rough between five and 10 times the revenue at the moment

insights.claim: Keen argues American AI has gone for brute force with as much energy as necessary while Chinese developers focus on cutting energy costs and running models on local machines, so Chinese AI will beat American AI and become an export, leaving America with both a bust and a technology loss.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: If efficiency beats scale, capital tied up in energy-intensive US datacentre buildouts is at risk while Chinese model efficiency becomes the exportable standard.
insights.quote: I've got a feeling it means Chinese AI is going to beat American AI

insights.claim: Keen argues that because the middle class grew out of the clerical bureaucracies Marx did not anticipate, AI capable of replacing clerical work could eliminate up to 70% of Western employment, forcing universal basic income, which China can deliver more easily than America by cutting the retirement age rather than sacking workers.
insights.speaker: Steve Keen
insights.so_what: Positions the political capacity to redistribute as the decisive variable in who captures AI gains, implying more social disruption risk in the US than in China.
insights.quote: then 70% of the employment in the west in western countries can disappear
